question: What is the Spring IoC container and what problem does it solve?

options.text: IoC container is Spring's built-in web server

IoC (Inversion of Control) container manages object lifecycle and wires dependencies automatically — instead of objects creating their dependencies, the container injects them, enabling loose coupling and testability
IoC container is a database connection pool manager
IoC stands for Input/Output Connector — it manages file I/O

explanation: Without IoC: `new UserService(new UserRepository(new DataSource(...)))` — classes are tightly coupled. With IoC: the container reads configuration (annotations, XML, Java config) and creates and wires beans. You receive dependencies injected, not created. Benefits: loose coupling (swap implementations), easier testing (inject mocks), centralized lifecycle management.

question: What are the three types of dependency injection in Spring?

options.text: Field injection, setter injection, constructor injection — Spring supports all three
XML injection, annotation injection, Java config injection
Bean injection, service injection, repository injection
Singleton injection, prototype injection, request injection

explanation: (1) Constructor injection: `@Autowired` on constructor (recommended) — dependencies are required, enables final fields, easy to test. (2) Setter injection: `@Autowired` on setter — optional dependencies, allows late injection. (3) Field injection: `@Autowired` on field (least recommended) — hides dependencies, harder to test without Spring. Spring team recommends constructor injection for mandatory dependencies.

question: What are Spring bean scopes?

options.text: Spring beans have only one scope: singleton
Singleton (default, one instance per container), Prototype (new instance each time), Request (per HTTP request), Session (per HTTP session), Application (per ServletContext)
Spring beans use Java's scope rules (local, instance, static)
Bean scope determines which package the bean is visible in

explanation: `@Scope("singleton")` (default): one shared instance per ApplicationContext. `@Scope("prototype")`: new instance on each `getBean()` call — Spring doesn't manage its full lifecycle after creation. `@Scope("request")`, `@Scope("session")`, `@Scope("application")`: web-only scopes. Caution: injecting a prototype bean into a singleton won't give a new prototype each time — use `Provider<T>` or `@Lookup`.

question: What is Spring AOP and what is an Aspect?

options.text: AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming) allows separating cross-cutting concerns (logging, transactions, security) from business logic via Aspects — applied transparently using proxies
AOP is Spring's API for Object Persistence
AOP is a testing framework for Spring beans
Aspects are Spring's name for configuration classes

explanation: AOP terminology: Aspect (module of cross-cutting concern), Advice (action at a join point: Before, After, Around, AfterReturning, AfterThrowing), JoinPoint (method execution), Pointcut (expression selecting join points), Weaving (applying aspects). Spring AOP uses JDK dynamic proxies (interface-based) or CGLIB (class-based). `@Transactional` is AOP under the hood.

question: What does `@Transactional` do in Spring?

options.text: @Transactional marks a class as a database entity
@Transactional wraps the method in a database transaction — starting one if none exists, committing on success, rolling back on RuntimeException (by default)
@Transactional is required for all Spring service methods
@Transactional makes a method thread-safe

explanation: Spring wraps `@Transactional` methods in a proxy. Default propagation: `REQUIRED` (join existing transaction or create new). Rollback triggers: `RuntimeException` (unchecked) by default — not checked exceptions unless `rollbackFor = Exception.class`. Common gotchas: (1) self-invocation bypasses proxy — @Transactional won't fire. (2) Method must be `public` (proxy limitation). (3) Exception must propagate — don't swallow it.

question: What is Spring Boot auto-configuration and how does it work?

options.text: Auto-configuration compiles Spring applications automatically without `javac`

Auto-configuration detects classes/jars on the classpath and automatically creates beans with sensible defaults — if you add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, a DataSource, EntityManagerFactory, and TransactionManager are configured automatically
Auto-configuration generates Spring XML configuration from code
Auto-configuration is disabled by default — enable with @EnableAutoConfiguration

explanation: `@SpringBootApplication` includes `@EnableAutoConfiguration`. Spring Boot scans `spring.factories` (or `AutoConfiguration.imports` in Boot 3+) for `@Configuration` classes with `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` etc. If DataSource class is on classpath and no DataSource bean exists, it creates one from `application.properties`. You can override any auto-configured bean by defining your own.

question: What is the difference between `@Controller` and `@RestController`?

options.text: @Controller is for traditional MVC (returns view names); @RestController is @Controller + @ResponseBody — methods return data serialized to JSON/XML directly
@RestController is for microservices; @Controller is for monoliths
@Controller requires XML configuration; @RestController uses annotations
They are identical — @RestController is just a shorter alias

explanation: `@Controller` marks a class as a Spring MVC controller. Methods return view names (resolved by ViewResolver) by default. Add `@ResponseBody` to a method to return data as response body. `@RestController` = `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody` on the class — all methods return data directly (JSON via Jackson by default). Use `@Controller` for server-side rendering (Thymeleaf), `@RestController` for REST APIs.

question: What are `@RequestMapping`, `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping` and related annotations?

options.text: @RequestMapping is for GET; @GetMapping is for POST — they handle different HTTP methods
@RequestMapping maps HTTP requests to methods (can specify method). @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping are shortcuts for specific HTTP methods
They are only for WebSocket endpoints
@RequestMapping is deprecated — only use @GetMapping and @PostMapping

explanation: `@RequestMapping(value="/users", method=RequestMethod.GET)` is the general form. `@GetMapping("/users")` is the shortcut. Can be combined with `@RequestParam`, `@PathVariable`, `@RequestBody`, `@RequestHeader`. At class level, `@RequestMapping("/api/v1")` sets a base path for all methods in the controller.

question: What is Spring Data JPA and what does `JpaRepository` provide?

options.text: Spring Data JPA is a standalone ORM framework separate from Hibernate
Spring Data JPA generates repository implementations at runtime from interface declarations — JpaRepository provides CRUD operations, pagination, sorting, and derived query methods
JpaRepository requires writing SQL queries for all operations
Spring Data JPA only works with PostgreSQL

explanation: `JpaRepository<T, ID>` provides: `save()`, `findById()`, `findAll()`, `delete()`, `count()`, pagination (`findAll(Pageable)`), sorting. Derived queries: `findByEmailAndStatus(String email, Status status)` — Spring generates the JPQL automatically from the method name. `@Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE ...")` for custom JPQL. `@Modifying` for update/delete queries.

question: What is `application.properties` vs `application.yml` and how does Spring Boot load configuration?

options.text: application.properties is for production; application.yml is for development

Both configure Spring Boot properties — .yml has hierarchical structure. Spring Boot loads: default → profile-specific (application-{profile}.yml) → external. @Value and @ConfigurationProperties bind values to beans
Only application.properties is supported — .yml requires a separate library
application.yml overrides application.properties only when both exist

explanation: Spring Boot loads configuration in priority order (later overrides earlier): default properties → application.properties/yml → profile-specific → command line args → environment variables. `@Value("${server.port:8080}")` injects a property with default. `@ConfigurationProperties(prefix="app")` binds a whole config subtree to a POJO. Profiles: `spring.profiles.active=prod` loads `application-prod.yml`.

question: What is Spring Boot Actuator?

options.text: Actuator is Spring's database connection pool
Spring Boot Actuator provides production-ready monitoring endpoints: /actuator/health, /actuator/metrics, /actuator/env, /actuator/beans, /actuator/loggers — all over HTTP or JMX
Actuator is Spring's AOP implementation
Actuator is a security module for authentication

explanation: Add `spring-boot-starter-actuator`. Default endpoint: `/actuator/health` (integration with load balancer health checks). Key endpoints: `/actuator/metrics/jvm.memory.used` (Micrometer metrics), `/actuator/env` (all properties), `/actuator/beans` (all Spring beans), `/actuator/loggers` (change log levels at runtime), `/actuator/threaddump`, `/actuator/heapdump`. Secure in production: expose only health by default, use Spring Security to protect others.

question: What is `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, and `@Controller` — are they different?

options.text: They are completely different annotations with distinct behaviors

@Component is the generic stereotype. @Service, @Repository, @Controller are specializations — all trigger component scanning and bean creation. @Repository additionally enables JPA exception translation
@Service creates beans with prototype scope; @Component creates singletons
@Repository is for MongoDB; @Component is for SQL databases

explanation: All are `@Component` specializations — detected by component scanning (`@ComponentScan`). Semantic differences: `@Service` (business logic — no extra behavior). `@Repository` (data access — enables Spring's PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor to translate native exceptions to Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy). `@Controller` (Spring MVC — enables request mapping processing). Use the most specific one for documentation and tooling.

question: What is `@Bean` vs `@Component` in Spring?

options.text: @Bean is deprecated; use @Component instead

@Component is a class-level annotation for Spring to manage; @Bean is a method-level annotation in a @Configuration class — used when you don't own the class (third-party) or need fine-grained creation control
@Bean creates prototype beans; @Component creates singletons
@Bean requires the class to implement BeanFactory

explanation: `@Component` (and stereotypes) annotate classes you own — Spring instantiates them via component scanning. `@Bean` annotates methods in `@Configuration` classes — Spring calls the method and registers the return value as a bean. Use `@Bean` for: third-party classes you can't annotate, complex creation logic, conditional bean registration. Both are singleton by default.

question: What is Spring Security and how do you configure basic authentication?

options.text: Spring Security is only for OAuth2 and JWT — not for basic auth

Spring Security is a framework for authentication and authorization — auto-configures HTTP Basic and form login. Customize by extending WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter (pre-Boot 2.7) or using SecurityFilterChain bean (Boot 3+)
Spring Security requires a database to store user credentials
Spring Security is disabled by default — must be explicitly enabled

explanation: Spring Boot auto-configures Spring Security if on classpath (generates a random password, enables HTTP Basic). Customize with a `SecurityFilterChain` bean: configure which endpoints require auth, which permit all, CSRF settings, session management, and authentication (in-memory, JDBC, LDAP, OAuth2). Use `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` for method-level security.

question: What is `@Conditional` and how does Spring Boot use it for auto-configuration?

options.text: @Conditional is used to create conditional branches in business logic

@Conditional creates beans only when specified conditions are met. Spring Boot uses: @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty, @ConditionalOnWebApplication — enabling smart auto-configuration
@Conditional is deprecated — use @Profile instead
@Conditional only works with @Component, not @Bean

explanation: Spring Boot's auto-configuration is built entirely on `@Conditional` variants: `@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)` — configure JPA only if DataSource is on classpath. `@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)` — don't override if user defined their own. `@ConditionalOnProperty("feature.enabled")` — activate by property. `@ConditionalOnWebApplication` — only in web context. Create your own conditions by implementing `Condition`.

question: What is `ResponseEntity<T>` in Spring MVC?

options.text: ResponseEntity is Spring's database response wrapper
ResponseEntity<T> represents a full HTTP response: status code, headers, and body — used when you need control over the response beyond just the body
ResponseEntity is required for all REST endpoints
ResponseEntity is deprecated — use @ResponseStatus instead

explanation: `ResponseEntity<User>` lets you set HTTP status, headers, and body: `ResponseEntity.ok(user)` (200 + body), `ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(user)` (201 + Location header), `ResponseEntity.notFound().build()` (404 + no body), `ResponseEntity.status(422).body(errorDetails)`. Use when you need fine-grained HTTP response control; use `@ResponseStatus` for simple fixed-status methods.

question: What is `@ExceptionHandler` and `@ControllerAdvice` in Spring?

options.text: @ExceptionHandler suppresses exceptions so they don't reach the client

@ExceptionHandler maps specific exceptions to HTTP responses in a controller. @ControllerAdvice applies exception handling globally across all controllers — used to build a consistent error response format
@ControllerAdvice is for AOP; @ExceptionHandler is for validation
They are only available in Spring Boot, not plain Spring MVC

explanation: `@ExceptionHandler(UserNotFoundException.class)` in a controller handles that exception for that controller only. `@RestControllerAdvice` (= `@ControllerAdvice` + `@ResponseBody`) handles exceptions globally. Best practice: one `@RestControllerAdvice` class with handlers for all exceptions, returning a consistent error DTO with status, message, timestamp, and traceId.

question: What is `@Valid` and bean validation in Spring?

options.text: @Valid triggers Spring to run the method and validate its result

@Valid on a method parameter triggers JSR-380 (Bean Validation) — annotations like @NotNull, @Size, @Email on the parameter's class fields are validated; ConstraintViolationException / MethodArgumentNotValidException on failure
@Valid marks a class as a Spring-managed bean
@Valid only works with String fields

explanation: Spring integrates with Hibernate Validator (JSR-380). Annotate DTO fields: `@NotNull`, `@NotBlank`, `@Size(min=1, max=50)`, `@Email`, `@Pattern`, `@Min`, `@Max`, `@Valid` (for nested objects). In controllers, `@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest req` triggers validation. On failure: `MethodArgumentNotValidException` — handle in `@ExceptionHandler` to return 400 with field errors.

question: What is Spring WebFlux and when would you use it over Spring MVC?

options.text: WebFlux is the same as Spring MVC — just a different name

WebFlux is Spring's reactive web framework built on Project Reactor — use for high-concurrency I/O-bound services where you need non-blocking I/O and back-pressure, avoiding thread-per-request blocking
WebFlux is only for streaming video content
WebFlux uses more threads than Spring MVC for better performance

explanation: Spring MVC: blocking I/O, thread-per-request (Servlet). Spring WebFlux: non-blocking I/O, event-loop model (Netty by default). Uses `Mono<T>` (0-1 result) and `Flux<T>` (0-N results). Benefits: handles more concurrent requests with fewer threads for I/O-bound work. Drawbacks: harder to reason about, reactive library must be used throughout the stack. MVC is simpler and usually sufficient — choose WebFlux for very high concurrency requirements.

question: What is the Spring `@Async` annotation and how does it work?

options.text: @Async makes the annotated method synchronous — blocking the caller until done
@Async causes the method to execute in a separate thread from the caller's thread pool — the caller returns immediately, getting a Future/CompletableFuture for the result
@Async is only for @Scheduled methods
@Async automatically handles transactions from the calling thread

explanation: Enable with `@EnableAsync` on a config class. Method must be `public` and called from OUTSIDE the class (self-invocation bypasses proxy). Returns `void`, `Future<T>`, or `CompletableFuture<T>`. Spring runs it on a configured `TaskExecutor`. Without custom config, uses a `SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor` (creates new thread per call — configure `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor` in production). Exceptions in void @Async methods go to `AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler`.

question: What is `@Cacheable` in Spring?

options.text: @Cacheable makes a method result available globally as a static variable

@Cacheable caches method return values — on subsequent calls with the same parameters, the cached value is returned without executing the method. Spring abstracts over multiple cache providers (Caffeine, Redis, EhCache)
@Cacheable is only for database query results
@Cacheable stores values in the Spring application context

explanation: Enable with `@EnableCaching`. `@Cacheable("users")` caches by all parameters by default; `key="#id"` specifies the cache key. `@CacheEvict("users")` clears entries. `@CachePut` always executes and updates cache. Configure a `CacheManager` bean for the provider (Caffeine for in-memory, Redis for distributed). Spring abstracts the cache — swap providers without changing code.

question: What is `@Scheduled` in Spring Boot?

options.text: @Scheduled starts an HTTP server for scheduled HTTP callbacks
@Scheduled runs a method on a fixed schedule — using fixedRate, fixedDelay, or cron expressions. Requires @EnableScheduling
@Scheduled is the same as @Async
@Scheduled can only be used in @Controller classes

explanation: Enable with `@EnableScheduling`. `@Scheduled(fixedRate = 5000)`: runs every 5 seconds (next execution starts 5s after last START). `@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 5000)`: 5 seconds after last COMPLETION. `@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * ?")`: standard cron expression (daily at 2am). By default runs on a single-threaded executor — configure `TaskScheduler` bean for thread pool. Long-running tasks block the scheduler.

question: What is the difference between `@SpringBootTest` and `@WebMvcTest` for testing?

options.text: @SpringBootTest is for unit tests; @WebMvcTest is for integration tests
@SpringBootTest loads the full ApplicationContext (integration test); @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers, filters, converters) with mocked services — faster and more focused
@WebMvcTest requires a running server; @SpringBootTest does not
They are identical — only the annotation name differs

explanation: `@SpringBootTest`: full context, can test whole application including database. `@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)`: only loads web layer, `@Service`/`@Repository` beans must be `@MockBean`'d. Use `MockMvc` to simulate HTTP requests without starting a real server. `@DataJpaTest`: JPA layer only with in-memory H2. `@MockBean`: replaces a bean in context with a Mockito mock.

question: What are Spring Profiles and how do you use them?

options.text: Spring Profiles are performance profiling tools built into Spring
Profiles allow different configurations for different environments (dev, test, prod). Beans can be activated per profile with @Profile; activate with spring.profiles.active property
Profiles are only for database configuration
Profiles replace environment variables in Spring Boot

explanation: `@Profile("dev")` on a `@Bean` or `@Configuration` class: only active when dev profile is active. Activate: `spring.profiles.active=prod` in `application.properties`, `-Dspring.profiles.active=prod` JVM arg, or `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` env var. Profile-specific files: `application-dev.yml` auto-loaded when dev profile is active. Use for environment-specific beans (H2 vs PostgreSQL DataSource, mock vs real services).

question: What is transaction propagation in Spring and what are the main propagation types?

options.text: Transaction propagation determines which database is used

Propagation controls how transactions behave when methods call each other: REQUIRED (join or create), REQUIRES_NEW (always new, suspends current), SUPPORTS (join if exists, else none), MANDATORY (must have existing), NEVER (must not have existing), NOT_SUPPORTED (always non-transactional)
All Spring methods share one transaction — propagation is automatic
Propagation only applies to read-only transactions

explanation: Key propagation types: `REQUIRED` (default): joins existing transaction; creates new if none. `REQUIRES_NEW`: always starts new transaction, suspends current — useful for audit logging that must commit even if caller rolls back. `SUPPORTS`: transactional if caller is, non-transactional otherwise. `NOT_SUPPORTED`: always non-transactional (suspends current). `MANDATORY`: must have existing transaction — throws if none. `NEVER`: must NOT have transaction.
